topic: Word Usage (Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension)

sections.title: Deep Semantic Understanding in Word Usage
sections.content: At Level 3, the usage of words must be understood on multiple levels. A single word may appear in literal, abstract, idiomatic, or even incorrect/fictitious collocations. To determine the correct usage, it is necessary to analyze the meaning of the word, the context of the sentence, and how the word is commonly used in English.

sections.title: Literal Meaning Usage
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the basic or direct meaning of the word. Step 2: Check whether the sentence is using the word in its physical or real-world sense. Step 3: Verify from the context whether the action or object described is actually possible. Step 4: If the meaning is direct and concrete, it represents literal usage. Example: 'The glass broke when it fell.' Here 'broke' is used in its literal sense.

sections.title: Abstract Meaning Usage
sections.content: Step 1: Understand the core meaning of the word. Step 2: Check whether it is used to describe an idea, emotion, or situation rather than a physical object. Step 3: Identify whether the meaning is symbolic or metaphorical. Step 4: Match it with the idea expressed in the sentence. Example: 'His words broke her confidence.' Here 'broke' is used in an abstract sense.

sections.title: Idiomatic Usage
sections.content: Step 1: Check whether the word is part of a phrase or expression. Step 2: Understand the meaning of the entire phrase instead of interpreting individual words. Step 3: Determine whether the phrase represents a commonly used idiom. Step 4: Accept that the meaning may differ from the literal interpretation. Example: 'Break the ice' means to start a conversation.

sections.title: Fictitious or Incorrect Collocation
sections.content: Step 1: Read the sentence and identify the key words. Step 2: Check whether the word forms a natural collocation. Step 3: If the combination sounds unnatural, compare it with standard language usage. Step 4: Verify both grammar and meaning. Step 5: If the phrase is not normally used in English, it may represent incorrect usage. Example: 'He manufactured a decision.' Here 'manufactured decision' is an incorrect collocation.

sections.title: Contextual Meaning Evaluation
sections.content: Step 1: Understand the meaning of the entire sentence or paragraph. Step 2: Identify the grammatical role of the word. Step 3: Evaluate whether the word is used in a literal, abstract, or idiomatic sense. Step 4: Choose the interpretation that best fits the logical and natural meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Interpreting idiomatic expressions literally. 2. Failing to recognize abstract meanings. 3. Accepting incorrect collocations that merely sound natural. 4. Relying only on dictionary meanings without considering context.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 3, word usage must be analyzed across multiple meaning layers. First examine the literal meaning, then consider abstract and idiomatic possibilities. Finally, confirm whether the collocation and context form a natural and logical expression.

tricks.title: Literal First Check
tricks.explanation: First check whether the word is used in its direct physical meaning.

tricks.title: Abstract Meaning Trick
tricks.explanation: If the word describes an idea, emotion, or condition, it may represent abstract usage.

tricks.title: Idiom Recognition Trick
tricks.explanation: If the word appears in a phrase, consider the meaning of the entire idiomatic expression.
tricks.example: Spill the beans = reveal a secret.

tricks.title: Collocation Familiarity Trick
tricks.explanation: Correct collocations are commonly used combinations in natural language.
tricks.example: Make a promise (correct), Create a promise (incorrect).

tricks.title: Context Layer Trick
tricks.explanation: Read the sentence carefully to determine whether the usage is literal, abstract, or idiomatic.
tricks.example: He carried the burden of responsibility.

tricks.title: Replacement Meaning Trick
tricks.explanation: Replace the word with a similar meaning word to test whether the sentence still makes sense.
tricks.example: Her voice broke → Her voice cracked.

tricks.title: Unnatural Phrase Detection
tricks.explanation: If the phrase sounds unnatural, it may represent a fictitious collocation.

tricks.title: Multi-Meaning Awareness
tricks.explanation: Many English words have multiple meanings, so choose the correct one based on context.
tricks.example: Light can mean illumination or not heavy.
